[i] The makers of Ring of Pain let you feel the warmth of Winnie’s intestines as you fill his hole. If you’re a roguelike deck builder enjoyer or have fantasised about feeding wild critters to a mutant bear, this game is a must play. [/i] [h1]📝 Main Pros, Cons, and Suggestions, followed by the Review:[/h1] 🟩 Pros: + The art and music are AAA quality + Different biomes, bosses, and virus types + Ability to grow your brain and virus blocks adds strategy + Viruses act as decks, intestines a map, and brains a battle board + Winnie mutates in real time as you acquire more mutations (cards) + The pendant has no right being so powerful (it does nothing, or does it?) + The fact that I can zoom out and see Winnie's internals is an amazing touch + Boss fights are well designed, each with unique abilities and modifiers to manage + Different types of attacks, such as bleed, counter, or piercing to keep combat engaging + Ain’t no way the hole in Winnie’s stomach isn’t meant to look like a forbidden coochie 🟥 Cons: - Can feel grindier earlier than others - Can’t see enemy stats before selecting a path (personal gripe, not a problem with the game) 🏷️ Suggestions: ~ I wish I could see the difficulty of encounters, or at least their HP, not only the rewards [h1] More Creative than Ring of Pain [/h1] The game begins with you, naked and afraid, talking about your gaping hole with your rabbit friend. It's like a chronically online X (Twitter) users NSFW Winnie the Pooh artwork fantasy came to life. In all seriousness, Winnie's Hole is an amazing game, bringing both creativity and uniqueness to an oversaturated genre. Winnie's Hole has you exploring his intestines (growth) and battling random creatures and critters (combat). His intestines act as the navigation map, where you use your Tetris shaped blocks to traverse and unlock new attacks, abilities, and upgrades, among other things. Be careful, though, you only start with 3 blocks so efficient navigation is required - Placing blocks outside his intestines may be quicker, but it costs health. Combat involves placing blocks in Winnie’s brain (a grid for your blocks) - Depending on the block used and the perks in your brain, you’ll perform actions like attacking, defending, grappling (among other things). It’s not complex, but it's very addictive, delivering a fast paced and easy to understand combat system with plenty of depth. There's a variety of mutations which act as cards (active skills) and perks (passive abilities) to play around with offers plenty of creativity in deck design. The charm comes from the ability to acquire new and upgrade existing blocks, as well as expanding your brain (grid). This system, coupled with the large variety of attacks and statuses, allows you to pull off some amazing combos. It’s unique, it’s refreshing, and it’s even better than Ring of Pain – I highly recommend it! [quote] Please consider following my [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/41005226/]Curation page[/url]. I cover a wide range of genres both paid and unpaid, providing unbiased opinions as well as regular giveaway events. [/quote] [B]Video Review[/b] https://youtu.be/g5znFkTMRzY [h2]Looking Past The Middle Finger To Disney...[/h2] This is a rough recommendation. On one hand, I really liked the demo. There was something compelling about it, likely the strong poetry in the original trailer, paired with the fact that the demo did not fully expose how poorly tuned the gameplay loop actually is. The RNG did not feel unbearable early on, and the game did not demand enough time to reveal its deeper problems. With deckbuilding roguelikes, progression is everything. You play, you fail, you win, you lose, and gradually you become stronger. This game does not work that way. You are always weak. You never feel powerful. And if you do manage to get strong, it comes with an asterisk. You must already know which encounters to avoid or you die anyway. You would never take a massive AoE build into a multi enemy fight like the bird and his trash mobs, since you end up empowering and enraging him to absurd levels, leading to massive damage against your pitiful 10 out of 10 life pool. On the flip side, bringing a single target build into encounters that spawn barricades and rocks that take no damage is just as bad. Those fights demand specific pull mechanics to drag the main target forward, and if you do not have them, the run is over. It is not challenging in a thoughtful way. It is just annoying. The body mutation system is another missed opportunity. There is so much potential here that the game barely taps into. Imagine something like trypophobia as a skin condition, attracting flies and maggots that you could then control, turning the virus itself into a summoner style build. That kind of visual and mechanical depth would add real identity to the system. Instead, it feels shallow and underdeveloped. Because the game is in Early Access, a lot of what appears in trailers and screenshots does not line up with the current experience. The virus placement mini game often shows four or more virus blocks empowering the player before moving to the next area, yet in actual gameplay, you are lucky to access four total, not counting the clearly pre placed ones shown in promotional material. It comes across as misleading. [h2]Conclusion[/h2] Outside of the novelty of the patent expiring and the ability to metaphorically stick it to Disney by mutilating an icon like Winnie the Pooh and friends, there simply is not enough substance here to justify picking it up. You are set up to fail repeatedly because the game actively resists letting you form a real build. Bleed plus sustain works, and there are likely others, but the odds of finding the right pieces when you actually need them are incredibly slim. If you fail to increase block size or brain size, you lose potential rotations and die. Bad starting hand pull. Dead. Poor healing or max HP rolls because the virus map screwed you. Tough luck. What makes it worse is the realization that once you finally win, there is nothing waiting for you. Four hours of failure leads to a single success, followed by the game saying, nice, do it again, but now with an even worse build to unlock slightly different builds. You repeat the same fights, in the same linear order, with no meaningful evolution. It is frustrating because the foundation shows promise, but the current experience feels hollow, punishing, and ultimately unrewarding.

I don't know why all these expired copyright based works want to turn the characters into murderers or horrific nightmares, but here's Winnie's Hole that's turned Xi-I mean, Winnie the Pooh into John Carpenter's The Thing. Also, I don't know why the genre 'rogue' is thrown about like it is, but Rogue is an actual game with a specific design. This game is nothing like Rogue. RNG alone does not make a game 'rogue like'. Maybe someone can tell me why I'm wrong. (edit: I'm being serious. This isn't bait. Please leave a comment telling me how this game is Rogue-like or Rogue-lite. I'm convinced people don't know what those terms mean) Anyway... Despite being a squatter on expired copyright, Winnie's Hole is inspired and has fantastic art. It's really well done. However I don't think the actual game itself works. I would describe it as very similar to card based battlers like Monster Train and Slay the Spire, but uses Tetris blocks (they're called tetronimoes!) instead of cards to activate abilities. The reason I don't recommend Winnie's Hole is because its not fun from being too hard. This isn't a skill issue. I can't exactly tell if its the RNG being too random or the very clearly unbalanced difficulty curve as you progress. Either way, a run always ends with Winnie getting crushed like a soda can by a powerful attack from a tanky enemy the player can't do anything about due to ♥♥♥♥ RNG, bad tile draws, and the near impossibility to pick an effective build. Another annoyance are unlockables. Normally, this is a feature that adds replay value and new ways to play. Its annoying AF in Winnie's Hole since you NEED to play and lose a few times just to get a set that doesn't fail as hard as the starter set. Its a shame since I really want to like this game. The aesthetic is fantastic and I want to play more, but the game itself needs a bit of work to make it more accessible. The RNG makes the game too ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to recommend.

Absolutely TEN OUT OF TEN, and I’m not even kidding. If you’ve ever wanted to live out your dream of being a microscopic villain with impeccable taste in strategy and chaos, Winnie’s Hole delivers harder than my immune system on flu season. You think deckbuilders are fun? Try deckbuilding while evolving inside Winnie’s brain and watching him squirm in the most wholesome way possible. This game makes tetromino puzzles, roguelikes, turn-based combat, and body horror hold hands and skip into the sunset singing campfire songs. Seriously. Every run feels like a clever crossover between a jam session in a science lab and a twisted cartoon fever dream. One minute you’re casually placing virus blocks like some kind of mad architect, the next you’re mutating poor Winnie into something that makes Cronenberg pause and say “Whoa, a bit much buddy.” It’s strategy, it’s comedy, it’s existential dread with ludicrous combo potential. The narrative? Dark and charming. The mechanics? Deep and satisfying. The concept? Absolutely bonkers. And best of all, it’s already a very positive Steam favorite, because who doesn’t want to experience body horror that feels like a hug from the inside? In short, this game doesn’t just break the mold, it infects it, mutates it, and makes its life choices look questionable in comparison. If you’ve got an appetite for strategy with a side of cute-meets-creepy, go get this now.

Winnie the Pooh Winnie the Pooh Grumbly wittle cubby no longer fluff he's... Winnie the Pooh Winnie the Pooh Silly Willy Nilly Devotee of M'Nagalah. And AS HIS FLESH DEVOLVES INTO FORMS UNKNOWN, NOVEL TUMORS, AN ENDLESS ABUNDANCE, TRANSMOGIFY, BLACKENED BEAR IN THE WOODS WITH A THOUSAND YOUNG. If we remember that the Hundred Acre Wood's anthropomorphized locals are an extension of the innocent playfulness of Christopher Robin's imagination, fueled by absent parents who have no interest in their son, I wonder what has happened in his personal life recently? When I play the game, I like to pretend that he has been sold to the Catholic church as a castrato, (commonly called a Eunuch) and he is currently recovering in his bed, waiting for some clergy to collect him. In fact, Winnie the Pooh originally takes place in the early 20th century, so this would make Christopher Robin the last purchased castrato. Unfortunately, by the late 18th century and early 19th century, the public has grown to hate these slaves of the church. Even though they were usually victims of abuse, the church's lurid and dodgy language made people think castrato were responsible for "luring men into homosexuality." I'm not saying this is canon, but I'm not going to let any of you believe it can't be.

Aside from the title being an immediate “ai yooo” moment, this is a surprisingly solid game. I tried the demo before the full release and had a lot more fun with it than I expected. The concept is weird in the right way, the dark humor works, and the roguelite side has enough going on to make runs feel engaging. The full release is also more difficult than I anticipated. There are more attacks, more options, and more things to keep in mind when building your stack, so it definitely asks for more strategy than the silly premise might suggest. If you like roguelites and dark humor, this one is worth checking out.

With all the slop that came out when Winnie-The-Pooh became public domain, I was a little wary seeing this on steam. That being said, it took an old, iconic character and gave it fresh ideas to the roguelite formula. The writing is creepy and fun, some choices you make will come back to haunt you in later runs, and there's variations in how you can set up Winnie to go about your runs. I'm satisfied with what I played, but knowing it's early access I'm looking forward to more content being added.
